analysis.one_liner: Phases out routine antibiotic feeding of livestock unless makers prove it doesn't breed drug resistance.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 128 cosponsors and a committee hearing in July 2009, but the House Energy and Commerce Committee never voted on it, and it died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug makers to prove, with a 'reasonable certainty of no harm,' that giving human-use antibiotics to healthy farm animals doesn't create resistant bacteria that endanger people. Absent that proof, FDA would have had to withdraw approval for those routine, non-therapeutic uses within two years. Sick animals could still be treated. The bill cited federal task force, National Academy of Sciences, and GAO findings linking antibiotic overuse in agriculture to rising drug resistance in people.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on antibiotics still working when they get pneumonia, food poisoning, or a post-surgery infection. The bill's findings cite studies estimating drug-resistant bacteria already cost the U.S. $4-5 billion a year, and note that about 70 percent of antibiotics sold in the U.S. go to farm animals without any sign of illness. It also lists more than 300 health, consumer, and agricultural organizations backing the approach, including the American Medical Association.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients who need antibiotics to still work

how_it_helps.text: Bars FDA approval of any new animal drug containing penicillin, tetracycline, macrolides, or other human-use antibiotics unless the maker shows a reasonable certainty of no harm from resistance caused by routine, non-therapeutic feeding [S2].
Requires withdrawal of existing approvals for routine antibiotic use in food-producing animals two years after enactment, unless the maker proves no harm to human health [S2].

Leaves legitimate disease treatment intact: the ban covers only use 'in the absence of any clinical sign of disease' for growth promotion or routine prevention, and it explicitly recognizes non-routine disease-prevention uses as legitimate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Confined livestock and poultry producers and the animal-drug companies whose products they buy, who would lose routine antibiotic feeding as a cheap substitute for hygiene and space, and would have to change husbandry practices or bear higher drug and compliance costs. Meat prices could rise somewhat as producers adjust.

drawbacks.text: The two-year withdrawal deadline would force rapid changes across farms that USDA surveys found routinely use feed antibiotics, and adjustment costs would fall on producers and eventually consumers [S3].

Routine disease prevention in large herds would be restricted along with growth promotion, which defenders of current practice argue is needed where animals are raised close together; the bill counters this by keeping therapeutic and documented-herd-disease uses available [S3].

The 'reasonable certainty of no harm' standard is a heavy proof burden, and the bill shifts the cost of the underlying safety science onto drug makers; some would argue FDA should handle this through its own review schedule rather than a statutory deadline [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but transitional: farmers and drug makers would spend money to change how animals are raised. The benefit is preserving the effectiveness of drugs modern medicine depends on, at a time when most farm-antibiotic approvals predate FDA's resistance reviews and no review schedule existed [S3]. The bill's design, allowing treatment of sick animals while ending routine dosing, addressed the main objection that antibiotics are needed for animal health.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, got a single hearing in July 2009, and then sat with no markup or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Introduced March 17, 2009 by Rep. Louise Slaughter and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Rules Committees [S5].
Referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on March 18, 2009 [S5].
The committee held one hearing on July 13, 2009; no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill attracted 128 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S4].
No vote ever occurred in either chamber, and the bill expired with the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Confined livestock producers and animal-drug makers, who kept routine antibiotic feeding without having to prove it safe for people. A similar bill was later introduced in following Congresses, but the drugs this bill targeted stayed on the market throughout.

for.name: Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 127 cosponsors within the Congress.

for.name: American Medical Association and other health and consumer groups
for.what_they_did: Supported phasing out routine antibiotic feeding in farm animals, per the bill's findings section.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and held one hearing; never brought the bill to a subcommittee or committee vote.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee took no markup or floor action on the bill after the July 2009 hearing.

against.name: Livestock and poultry producers and animal-drug makers
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory phase-outs of non-therapeutic antibiotic use in farm animals.

sides.party_line_note: All 128 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where the split could be recorded.

industries.note: The bill would force them to prove human-safety for routine feeding of human-use antibiotics or lose approval for those uses within two years. Their revenue depends on continued non-therapeutic sales, the very use the bill targets as a driver of resistance.

Routine antibiotic feeding substitutes for hygiene, space, and slower growth in crowded operations; the bill would end that practice. Cheap dosing lowers their costs while externalizing the cost of resistance onto patients and the health system.

Producers already raising animals without routine antibiotics would face a level field, since competitors could no longer use routine dosing to cut costs. The bill's findings list sustainable-agriculture groups among its backers.
